body:
What is wind energy?

Wind energy is the kinetic energy possessed by moving air. A wind turbine captures part of this energy and converts it into electricity. Wind is a renewable resource because the atmospheric processes responsible for its formation continue naturally.

Wind does not provide the same amount of energy everywhere or at every moment. Its usefulness for electricity generation depends on local wind speed, direction, consistency and the physical conditions of the site.

Wind power: The use of the kinetic energy of moving air to perform mechanical work or generate electricity.

How does wind originate?

The Sun heats the Earth's surface unevenly. Land, water bodies and different surfaces absorb and release heat at different rates. This produces differences in air temperature and pressure. Air moves in response to pressure differences, producing wind. Earth's rotation and the shape of the land influence the direction and movement of winds.

At the elementary level, air generally tends to move from regions of higher pressure towards regions of lower pressure. The actual direction of wind is modified by Earth's rotation, surface friction and local geographical features.

Wind is therefore an indirect form of solar energy. A wind turbine does not require sunlight to fall directly on it, but the atmospheric movement supplying its energy is largely sustained by solar heating.

Where are wind resources favourable?

Wind turbines are particularly useful where the wind is sufficiently strong and reasonably consistent over time. Suitable locations often include coastal belts, open plains, exposed hills, mountain passes and some offshore areas.

  • Coastal regions: Land-sea temperature differences and regional wind systems can create useful wind conditions.
  • Mountain passes and exposed ridges: Landforms may concentrate or accelerate moving air, although turbulence can also occur.
  • Open plains: Fewer nearby obstructions may allow relatively unobstructed airflow.
  • Offshore areas: Winds over the sea are often stronger and less turbulent than winds over obstructed land, although conditions vary by location.

A windy location is not automatically a suitable wind-farm site. Wind patterns must be measured at relevant heights over a sufficiently representative period. Seasonal changes, extreme weather, access and environmental restrictions also matter.

Wind energy potential in India

India has important wind resources in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and several other states. Gujarat is especially relevant because of its long coastline and suitable areas in Kachchh and Saurashtra.

The National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE), under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, undertakes wind-resource assessment. Its estimates depend on the assessment height and assumptions used to identify technically suitable locations.

India's assessed wind potential

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy's Annual Report 2024–25 reports an assessed gross wind-power potential of 1,163.85 GW for India at 150 m above ground level. The corresponding assessment for Gujarat is 180.79 GW. These are resource-potential estimates reported for the 2024–25 publication period, not installed generating capacities or actual electricity production.

This distinction is essential. A location may have a high assessed wind potential even though only part of it has been developed. Similarly, a turbine's installed capacity states its rated generating capability, not the electricity it produces continuously.

Earlier uses and modern applications

Traditional windmills used moving air to grind grain or lift water. Modern wind turbines primarily generate electricity. A single turbine can serve a local requirement, while many turbines installed together form a wind farm supplying electricity to a larger network.

Prelims focus

  • Wind energy is the kinetic energy of moving air and is indirectly derived from solar heating.
  • Coastal regions, open plains, exposed ridges and mountain passes can offer favourable wind resources.
  • Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are important Indian wind-resource states.
  • NIWE assesses wind resources in India.
  • The MNRE Annual Report 2024–25 gives India's gross assessed wind potential at 150 m as 1,163.85 GW, including 180.79 GW for Gujarat.
  • Trap: Assessed potential, installed capacity and actual electricity generated are different quantities.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, 2018–19 edition, p. 34; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, pp. 82–83; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Annual Report 2024–25, Chapter 4, Section 4.1.2 and Table 4.1, p. 33; U.S. Department of Energy, How Do Wind Turbines Work?, section on wind formation; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Wind Energy: Origin, Resource Distribution and Indian Potential

body:
How a wind turbine generates electricity

A wind turbine converts the kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy. It does so through the rotation of specially shaped blades connected to a generator.

Modern turbine blades are shaped somewhat like aircraft wings. As wind flows around a blade, differences in pressure and the aerodynamic forces acting on it produce a turning effect. Aerodynamic lift is the principal force used by most modern utility-scale wind turbines.

The blades rotate a central hub. Together, the blades and hub form the rotor. The rotor drives a shaft or other mechanical connection to the generator, which converts rotational mechanical energy into electricity.

The basic energy conversion is kinetic energy of wind → rotational mechanical energy → electrical energy. Wind turbines do not produce electricity by burning wind or by converting sunlight directly through solar cells.

Main components of a modern wind turbine

ComponentFunction
BladesCapture energy from moving air through aerodynamic forces.
Hub and rotorConnect the blades and transfer their rotation.
Main shaftTransmits mechanical rotation towards the generator.
GearboxIn many designs, increases rotational speed before the generator.
GeneratorConverts mechanical rotation into electrical energy.
NacelleEnclosure at the top of the tower containing major working equipment.
TowerSupports the rotor and nacelle at a useful height.
Yaw systemTurns the nacelle of suitable horizontal-axis designs to face the wind.
Pitch systemAdjusts blade angle to control energy capture and protect the rotor.
AnemometerMeasures wind speed.
Wind vaneMeasures wind direction.

Gearbox and direct-drive turbines

In a geared turbine, a gearbox increases the relatively slow rotational speed of the rotor to a speed suitable for the generator. A direct-drive turbine connects the rotor to a generator designed to operate without this gearbox.

Both arrangements produce electricity through a generator. Therefore, a gearbox is common but not an essential component of every wind turbine.

Yaw control, pitch control and protection

The yaw system adjusts the direction of the nacelle so the rotor can face the wind in a typical upwind horizontal-axis turbine. The pitch system changes the angle of the blades to regulate their aerodynamic action. A controller monitors operating conditions and may stop the turbine when the wind becomes dangerously strong. Braking and blade-feathering arrangements help protect the machine.

Yaw and pitch perform different functions: yaw changes the orientation of the turbine relative to wind direction, while pitch changes the angle of the blades themselves.

Horizontal-axis and vertical-axis wind turbines

Horizontal-axis wind turbines rotate around an approximately horizontal axis. They are the predominant design in large wind farms and commonly have 3 blades. Their rotor is generally oriented towards the wind.

Vertical-axis wind turbines rotate around a vertical axis. Several designs can accept wind from different horizontal directions without rotating the entire turbine to face the wind. They are less common in large utility-scale wind farms.

Windmill versus wind turbine: A traditional windmill commonly uses rotation directly for tasks such as grinding grain or pumping water. An electricity-generating wind turbine uses the captured rotation to drive a generator.

Why wind speed matters so much

The energy available in wind depends on wind speed, air density and the area swept by the rotor blades. For the same air density and swept area, the power available in the wind varies approximately with the cube of wind speed.

For example, if wind speed doubles while the other conditions remain unchanged, the kinetic power available in the moving air becomes 8 times as large. This is a relationship concerning the energy available in the wind, not a guarantee that a real turbine will always produce 8 times as much electricity.

The actual electrical output is limited by turbine characteristics and controls:

  • Below cut-in speed: The wind is insufficient for useful electricity generation.
  • Between cut-in and rated speed: Electrical output generally increases as wind speed rises.
  • At and above rated speed: The turbine regulates output near its rated maximum over a suitable wind-speed range.
  • At cut-out speed: The turbine may shut down to avoid damage from excessively strong wind.

Cut-in, rated and cut-out speeds are not identical for all turbine models.

Prelims focus

  • Rotor = blades and hub; generator = component that produces electricity.
  • Nacelle houses major working components, while the tower supports the assembly.
  • Anemometer measures speed; wind vane measures direction.
  • Yaw controls orientation; pitch controls blade angle.
  • Some turbines have gearboxes, while direct-drive turbines do not require them.
  • Trap: Stronger wind does not guarantee continuously increasing electrical output because turbines have rated and cut-out operating limits.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, How Do Wind Turbines Work?, sections on operation and turbine types, 9 June 2020; U.S. Department of Energy, Explore a Wind Turbine — Text Version, sections on blades, rotor, nacelle, yaw, pitch, gearbox, generator and controller; U.S. Department of Energy, How Do Wind Turbines Survive Severe Weather and Storms?, section The Power Curve; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 14, Sources of Energy, wind-energy discussion; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The rotor captures wind energy; the generator converts its rotation into electricity.

pictures.alt: Doubling wind speed gives 8 times available wind power, while turbine output rises, levels off at rated power, then shuts down at cut-out.

title: Wind Turbines: Components, Working Principle and Power Output

body:
What is a wind farm?

A wind farm is a group of wind turbines located in an area suitable for wind-energy generation. Each turbine converts wind energy into electricity. The electricity produced by the turbines can be collected and supplied for local use or to the wider electricity network.

Wind farms may be developed on land or in suitable water bodies. The turbine's basic working principle remains the same, but the location creates different opportunities and constraints.

Onshore and offshore wind systems

FeatureOnshore windOffshore wind
LocationOn land, including plains, ridges and coastal areas.In the sea or other suitable large water bodies.
Wind conditionsDepend strongly on terrain, vegetation and nearby obstructions.Often stronger and less turbulent, but highly site-dependent.
ConstructionNeeds suitable land, access roads and foundations.Needs marine foundations or floating support and specialised installation.
AccessUsually easier for routine maintenance.More difficult because of distance, waves and weather.
Environmental concernsBirds, bats, land habitats, noise and nearby communities.Marine ecosystems, birds, fishing activity and navigation.
Electricity connectionRequires suitable access to the electricity network.Requires a connection from the offshore site to land.

Offshore development may provide access to valuable wind resources, especially near coastal demand centres. However, it must account for sea depth, seabed conditions, marine traffic, fishing activity and construction conditions. Offshore wind is not automatically suitable along every part of a coastline.

Offshore wind potential near Gujarat

NIWE has identified 8 potential offshore wind zones off Gujarat and 8 off Tamil Nadu through preliminary assessment. Important assessment areas include the Gulf of Khambhat near Gujarat and the Gulf of Mannar near Tamil Nadu.

These are identified potential zones, not a statement that 16 offshore wind farms have been commissioned. Resource surveys and development assessments are distinct from operating projects. This is the status described on NIWE's offshore development information consulted on 16 November 2026.

Why wind generation varies

Wind energy is variable because the speed and direction of air movement change over hours, days and seasons. A wind farm may generate substantial electricity during a windy period but very little when winds are weak.

In India, seasonal wind systems such as the monsoon influence wind availability in several regions. Local conditions, however, must be assessed separately; no single seasonal pattern describes every turbine location.

The following distinctions are useful:

  • Installed capacity: The rated generating capacity of the turbines.
  • Actual generation: The electricity produced during a particular period.
  • Capacity factor: Actual electricity generation over a period divided by the electricity that would have been produced if the plant operated at rated capacity throughout that period.

Capacity factor measures utilisation over time. It is not the same as the efficiency of converting the energy in the wind into electricity.

Wind forecasts, coordination with other sources of power and energy-storage systems can help manage changing output. A normal wind turbine does not store the wind that passes through it.

Environmental and community impacts

Wind turbines do not burn fossil fuels while generating electricity and therefore avoid direct combustion emissions during operation. Nevertheless, wind-power development can affect wildlife, landscapes and communities.

Effects on birds and bats

Birds and bats may collide with rotating turbine blades. The level of risk depends on the species, local habitat, migration routes, turbine placement and operating conditions. Disturbance and habitat modification can also occur during construction.

Possible measures include careful assessment of wildlife movement, avoiding especially sensitive habitats and reducing turbine operation during identified high-risk periods. Such measures can reduce risks but cannot guarantee that all collisions will be prevented.

Effects on nearby communities

Onshore turbines can produce audible noise and moving shadows, known as shadow flicker, when sunlight passes through rotating blades. Turbine foundations, roads and associated facilities also require land. In some agricultural areas, cultivation or grazing can continue around wind turbines, although this depends on the layout and local conditions.

Appropriate distances from settlements, careful layout, environmental assessment, consultation and fair treatment of affected land users are important elements of responsible siting.

Offshore environmental concerns

Offshore projects may disturb marine habitats during construction. Underwater noise, seabed work, effects on fishing activity and conflicts with navigation routes require particular attention. Assessments should consider marine wildlife, existing sea uses and the conditions of the proposed site.

Renewable does not mean impact-free. Wind energy reduces dependence on fuel combustion during electricity generation, but its environmental and social effects still need assessment and management.

Prelims focus

  • Onshore turbines are installed on land; offshore turbines are installed in suitable water bodies.
  • Offshore winds are often less turbulent, but marine construction and maintenance are more difficult.
  • NIWE identifies 8 potential offshore wind zones each off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.
  • Wind generation varies with weather and seasons; installed capacity is not continuous output.
  • Bird and bat collisions, habitat effects, noise, shadow flicker and community concerns are relevant wind-farm impacts.
  • Trap: An identified offshore wind zone is not necessarily an operating offshore wind farm.

[Sources: National Institute of Wind Energy, Offshore Wind Development, sections Offshore Wind Power Development and Marine Spatial Planning, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Offshore Wind, section Offshore Wind Resource Assessment, consulted 16 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Frequently Asked Questions about Wind Energy, sections on wildlife and human impacts, consulted 16 November 2026; U.S. Geological Survey, Ultrasonic Deterrents Provide No Additional Benefit over Curtailment in Reducing Bat Fatalities at an Ohio Wind Energy Facility, 8 May 2025; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 3, p. 34.]

pictures.caption: Responsible siting considers wind resources alongside wildlife and community risks.

title: Wind Farms: Onshore and Offshore Systems, Variability and Environmental Impacts
